title: Postal Code Centroid Calculator: Center of Codes
description: Find the centre of gravity of a list of ZIP or postal codes with the Postal Code Centroid Calculator — spherical centroid plus each code's distance. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the centroid of ZIPs 10001 (New York), 60601 (Chicago) and 90210 (Beverly Hills) falls near 39.0, −94.8 in Missouri — the spherical centre of the three, computed by this page's method.
quick_answer: The Postal Code Centroid Calculator finds the centre of gravity of a pasted list of ZIP or postal codes: the point on the sphere that minimises the average straight-line distance to all of them. Paste the codes, press find, and read the centre, its nearest place, and each code's distance.

examples.label: Example · Why not average the latitudes?

body.t: Flat averaging of lat/lon distorts near the poles and the date line. This calculator averages directions on the sphere (the 3D vector method), then converts back — the difference is small for one county, real for one continent.

faq: How is the centre computed?
By the spherical (3D vector) average of the codes' centroid points — the point minimising average straight-line distance on the sphere — not by flat latitude/longitude averaging.
Which countries work?
ZIP and postal systems the resolver covers — US ZIPs are the home case; many other countries' postal codes resolve too, with coverage following the underlying open data.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — the codes are the only input.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Postal centroid datasets differ by source and vintage; another resolver's point for the same code can sit a little apart, nudging the centre.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No.
One code dominates my list — can I weight?
The centroid treats codes equally; repeat a code to weight it, or trim the list. The distances table shows each code's pull honestly.
The centre is in a lake or nowhere.
Centres are geometry, not venues. Treat the nearest place in the result as the practical meeting town.
Duplicate codes?
Fine — duplicates act as votes, which is sometimes exactly what attendance weighting should do.
Codes that fail to resolve?
They are reported rather than silently dropped, so your list's coverage is visible — check formats and country assumptions first.
Can I exclude outliers?
Trim the list and rerun — the centre's shift between runs is itself the outlier's measured pull. Deliberate, visible, honest.
Thousands of codes?
Paste in reasonable batches; the method scales, but a territory-scale job belongs in a GIS with this page's method as the sanity check.
